title: Find Peak Element
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning every index directly versus a binary search guided by the slope between adjacent elements.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: A peak element is an element strictly greater than its neighbors. Given an integer array nums, where nums[-1] and nums[n] are treated as negative infinity, find any peak element and return its index. If the array contains multiple peaks, returning the index of any one of them is acceptable.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["ANY peak is acceptable, not necessarily the largest one","Binary search can be used, even though the array is not sorted"],["The comparison between two adjacent elements always points toward a guaranteed peak in one direction","A binary search that follows the \"uphill\" direction at every step"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Find any index whose value is strictly greater than both of its neighbors (treating positions before the start and after the end as negative infinity), and return that index.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Any Hilltop While Walking Blindfolded
blocks.text: Picture walking along a bumpy trail blindfolded, only able to feel whether the ground ahead slopes up or down. Always stepping toward the uphill direction is guaranteed to eventually reach some hilltop, not necessarily the tallest one, but a genuine local peak.

blocks.caption: The slope between two adjacent elements always points toward a guaranteed peak

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: nums = [1,2,3,1]
Index 2 (value 3) is greater than both its neighbors, 2 and 1, so it is a peak.
Both index 1 (value 2) and index 5 (value 6) are valid peaks; returning either is accepted.
Edge case: a strictly increasing or decreasing array
The last element is a peak in a strictly increasing array (since the position past the end counts as negative infinity), and the first element is a peak in a strictly decreasing array.
5. How Should We Think?
Before scanning the whole array, notice that comparing just two adjacent elements always guarantees a peak exists somewhere in one specific direction.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If nums[mid] is less than nums[mid plus 1], the sequence is rising at that point, so following it further right must eventually reach a peak (even the very last element, bounded by negative infinity past the end).

Observation 2: If nums[mid] is greater than nums[mid plus 1], the sequence is falling, so mid itself might be a peak, or a peak exists somewhere to its left, bounded by negative infinity before the start.

Observation 3: Either way, half of the remaining search space can be discarded at every step, exactly a binary search, just guided by slope direction instead of value comparison to a target.

Observation 4: The search converges once the range narrows to a single index, which must be a valid peak by the same logic applied at every step.
This leads directly to a binary search that discards the "downhill" half of the array at every step, guaranteed to converge on a genuine peak.
6. Brute Force Solution
Scan every index directly, checking whether it is strictly greater than both of its neighbors.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every index i from 0 to n minus 1, treat out-of-bounds neighbors as negative infinity.
Check whether nums[i] is greater than both its left and right neighbor.
Return the first index that satisfies this.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check every index directly against both neighbors

codes.python:
def find_peak_element(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    for i in range(n):
        left = nums[i - 1] if i > 0 else float('-inf')
        right = nums[i + 1] if i < n - 1 else float('-inf')
        if nums[i] > left and nums[i] > right:      # check every index directly
            return i
    return -1

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Out-of-bounds neighbors are treated as negative infinity, matching the problem's own boundary convention directly.
Every index is checked independently, with no use of the fact that a peak's existence can be inferred from slope direction alone.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), every index may need to be checked.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: a full linear scan is not actually necessary, since the direction of a single comparison between two adjacent elements is enough to guarantee which half of the array a peak lies in, an opportunity for a logarithmic search that the brute force does not exploit.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why a linear scan is not required: unlike a search for a specific value, this search only needs to follow the local slope, and that slope always guarantees a peak exists in a determinable direction.

What rule decides which half to search: comparing nums[mid] to nums[mid plus 1]; if it is rising, search the right half; if it is falling, mid could itself be the peak, so keep it in the search and move to the left half.

The core idea: binary search using the slope between nums[mid] and nums[mid plus 1] to decide which half is guaranteed to contain a peak, converging on a single valid index.

Binary search with two pointers. At each step, compare nums[mid] to nums[mid plus 1]. If nums[mid] is smaller, a peak is guaranteed to the right, so move the left pointer past mid. Otherwise, mid could be a peak itself, so keep the search including mid and move the right pointer to mid. Stop when the two pointers meet.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: binary search following the slope toward a guaranteed peak

blocks.text: Why This Works

If nums[mid] is less than nums[mid plus 1], the sequence is still climbing, so a peak is guaranteed somewhere from mid plus 1 onward, all the way to the boundary at negative infinity. If nums[mid] is greater, either mid is itself a peak, or the true peak lies further left, either way it is safe to keep mid in the search range and discard everything to its right. This invariant holds at every step, guaranteeing convergence on a genuine peak.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n), the search range halves at every step.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Find Peak Element shows that binary search does not require a globally sorted array, only a local comparison that reliably points toward a valid answer in one direction is needed.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming binary search requires full sorted order, missing that a directional guarantee from a local comparison is sufficient here.
Comparing nums[mid] to nums[mid minus 1] instead of nums[mid plus 1], which flips the direction logic and can miscompute the boundary.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explaining why the slope between two adjacent elements guarantees a peak in one direction, even without full sorted order, is the key insight to state before writing any binary search code.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "the array is not sorted, how can binary search apply", think: a local comparison between two adjacent elements still guarantees a peak exists in a specific direction.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this generalize to a 2D grid, finding a peak greater than all four neighbors?
Why does this technique not require the array to have a unique peak?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "search on a monotonic property, not a sorted array" binary search variant.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n) time; the optimized binary search runs in O(log n) time. Both use O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: binary search guided by local slope direction, not a globally sorted order.
Core Idea: comparing nums[mid] to nums[mid plus 1] always guarantees a peak exists in one determinable direction, letting half the search space be discarded every step.
Time: O(n) for the brute force, O(log n) for the optimized binary search.
Most Important Observation: binary search only requires a directional guarantee from a local comparison, not full sorted order.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once it is recognized that binary search applies here at all.
One line memory trick: follow the uphill slope; it always leads to some peak.
